ground.purpose: The field the board and canvas sit on — the outermost of four surfaces.

surface.purpose: The sidebar, a card face, the panel, a popover.

surface-2.purpose: A column body, a rail input, a hovered table row, a canvas band.

surface-3.purpose: A count badge, a button on hover, a progress track.

ink.purpose: Every title, value and piece of body copy.

ink-2.purpose: Control labels and secondary values; brightens to ink on hover.

ink-3.purpose: Every label, key, count, meta line and excerpt — the ground state of annotation.

rule.purpose: Every boundary between regions, at exactly 1px.

rule-2.purpose: An interactive edge: an input, a popover, a hovered card.

dot.purpose: The canvas dot grid, and nothing else.

accent.purpose: The app's one voice: focus, selection, drop target, active filter, unsaved mark, primary button.

accent-soft.purpose: The accent's only fill — hovered drop column, bulk bar ground, focus pill. Never text.

ok.purpose: A finished reference, a filled progress bar.

warn.purpose: Unsaved state, a deadline landing today.

bad.purpose: A failure, a blocked left border, an open reference, an overdue deadline.

rel-parent.purpose: Decomposition edges on the canvas — the default spine.

rel-blocks.purpose: Blocking edges, the only edge kind with a text label. Light mode leaves the palette deliberately: red1 is illegible on white and red3 too dark for an edge.

hue-red.purpose: Chip text for waiting_on — the only facet whose presence is itself a warning.

hue-orange.purpose: Chip text for priority — what you intend to do next.

hue-green.purpose: Chip text for status — lifecycle, and nothing else.

hue-pink.purpose: Chip text for layer; the one family that also carries weight 600.

hue-red-bg.purpose: Chip fill for waiting_on, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

hue-orange-bg.purpose: Chip fill for priority, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

hue-yellow-bg.purpose: Chip fill for domain, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

hue-green-bg.purpose: Chip fill for status, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

hue-blue-bg.purpose: Chip fill for tech, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

hue-purple-bg.purpose: Chip fill for project, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

hue-pink-bg.purpose: Chip fill for layer, diluted by --chip-tint in light mode.

display.purpose: The vault gate's heading — the only full-page title in the app, and the only place type is large.

headline.purpose: The open record's title in the card panel. The largest type in normal use.

lg.purpose: The title textarea while editing, and the sort-direction arrow.

root.purpose: `body`: an inheritance root, not a used size. Almost nothing renders at it.

lede.purpose: The vault gate's opening paragraph, at a 60ch measure.

title.purpose: A record's title on a face, in a column or on the canvas. Two-line clamp on a canvas node.

body.purpose: The working size: buttons, inputs, table cells, reference rows, panel prose. The 14px on body is an inheritance root, not a used size.

body-sm.purpose: One step down for anything in a long vertical list: filter rows, rail selects, excerpts, kv values.

sm.purpose: Small buttons, inline code, the date input, the bulk-bar count.

xs.purpose: Tiny buttons, column counts, cluster labels, table numbers.

meta.purpose: A face's meta line, and the panel's kv keys in uppercase.

chip.purpose: Every facet chip and link chip.

label.purpose: The signature. Panel section heads, table headers, lane heads, rail labels. Tracking widens with prominence: 0.1em in rails and tables, 0.13em in the panel, 0.14em at the gate.

micro.purpose: Canvas edge labels, badge counts, a link chip kind prefix.

shadows.name: panel
shadows.purpose: The card panel, thrown leftward from the right edge it is docked to.

shadows.name: popover
shadows.purpose: Portalled menus — furthest from the plane, so they cast furthest.

shadows.name: picker
shadows.purpose: The record picker: smaller throw, higher opacity, because it is a modal over a scrim.

shadows.name: floating-bar
shadows.purpose: The bulk bar, which exists only while a selection does.

shadows.name: toolbar
shadows.purpose: The canvas toolbar — lightest, because it rests on the canvas rather than over content.

shadows.name: selection-ring
shadows.purpose: NOT elevation. A stroke drawn outside the selected card, because its border is already spoken for.

shadows.name: drop-line-top
shadows.purpose: NOT elevation. The reorder drop indicator above a card.

shadows.name: drop-line-bottom
shadows.purpose: NOT elevation. The reorder drop indicator below a card.

shadows.name: scrim
shadows.purpose: The panel scrim. A fill, not a shadow, but it belongs to the same depth vocabulary.

motion.name: shell-collapse
motion.purpose: The sidebar collapsing to 38px. One of only two transitions in the stylesheet.

motion.name: rail-width
motion.purpose: A rail control resizing. The other of the two.

motion.name: doctrine
motion.purpose: There are no keyframes. Regrouping, re-sorting and filtering are instant; motion is permitted only where a mouse gesture would feel broken without it — dragging a card, panning or zooming the canvas, collapsing the rail.

narrative.overview:
*Terminal* supplies the dense, text-first grammar and the xoria lineage. *Drafting* supplies projection, annotation, hierarchy and technical precision. Not a retro terminal wearing blueprint decoration — a working drawing made interactive.

The palette is xoria256, Dmitriy Zotikov's pastel Vim scheme, taken whole. Nothing is interpolated: every value in the stylesheet is a literal from estilo/palettes/xoria256.yml. The scheme is dark-first and has no light neutrals, so the dark theme *is* xoria and the light theme is derived from it — the same seven hue families, using the dark shades as ink where the light shades would disappear on white.

Two things make this a drawing rather than a dashboard. First, colour is notation. Each facet axis owns one hue family, mapped from xoria's own syntax roles — priority is Number (orange), status is PreProc (green), project is Type (purple), tech is Statement (blue), layer is Identifier (pink) — so a chip's hue tells you which axis it is before you read the word. Second, the surface is still. Two CSS transitions exist in 48 KB of stylesheet and both animate a width; there are no keyframes. A surface that sits open on a second monitor all day is a readout, and a readout that moves is a distraction.

The precision is literal, not atmospheric. The record mark beside every title carries two translateY constants — 0.03em and -0.058em — derived from where each glyph’s ink actually centres against lowercase text. They are measurements, not taste.
keyCharacteristics: Dark-first xoria256, taken literally; light derived from the same seven families
Monospace for everything the app says, sans for everything a human typed
A nine-step type scale in which the largest working size is 16px and the signature size is 9.5px
One hue family per facet axis; hueless chips for facets that are hints rather than identity
Four tonal surfaces and 1px hairlines — depth by layering, shadows only for what genuinely floats
Still at rest: instant regrouping, motion only where a mouse gesture would feel broken without it
Desktop-only by construction; no breakpoints, no responsive system, no top bar
Precise and unadorned: no fill, stroke or radius that is not load-bearing

rules.name: The One Hue Per Axis Rule
rules.body: A facet axis owns exactly one hue family, and a hue family serves exactly one axis. Adding a facet means claiming a family, not picking a colour you like. Two axes in one family destroys the property the whole palette exists for: that a chip's colour is legible before its text is.

rules.name: The Hints Are Hueless Rule
rules.body: A facet that is a hint rather than an identity gets no hue at all — transparent fill, rule border, ink-3 text, italic for energy. If a new facet does not deserve a hue family, it does not get a diluted one; it recedes.

rules.name: The Dilution Rule
rules.body: --chip-tint is 42% in light and 100% in dark. Xoria's light shades are saturated pastels: full strength is fine on one chip and loud on eight stacked down a column, so light mode mixes the fill toward the surface with color-mix. Any new tinted surface goes through --chip-tint, not a hand-picked value.

rules.name: The App Voice Rule
rules.body: The accent marks live state and the app speaking — focus, selection, a drop target, an active filter, an unsaved view, a count the app computed. It never marks data structure. A property of a record is drawn in that facet’s own hue.

rules.name: The Mono Label Rule
rules.body: If a human typed it, it is sans; if the app is naming, counting or annotating something, it is mono. There is no third case, and the division is what makes a screen with nine type sizes read as two voices rather than nine.

rules.name: The Tabular Number Rule
rules.body: Any number that can change while its neighbours stay put carries font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums. A count that shifts width when it increments is a count you cannot read at a glance.

rules.name: The Measured Glyph Rule
rules.body: A glyph placed in a text run is measured, not eyeballed. The record marks sit at 0.8em with line-height: 1, baseline-aligned, plus a per-glyph translateY derived from where its ink actually centres.

rules.name: The Desktop-Only Rule
rules.body: The only @media query in the stylesheet is prefers-color-scheme. There are no breakpoints, because the surface is a second monitor and never a phone. Overlays clamp themselves with min(px, vw) and that is the whole of the adaptive behaviour.

rules.name: The No Chrome Rule
rules.body: New global controls go into a rail block or the footer. The app has no top bar and adding one would cost 40px of board height on every shape to serve whichever shape needed it.

rules.name: The Flat Plane Rule
rules.body: Anything that lives in the layout is flat: a fill, a hairline, and no shadow. A shadow is permission to leave the plane, and only five elements have it.

rules.name: The Stroke-As-Shadow Rule
rules.body: Two box-shadow declarations are not shadows and must not be read as elevation: 0 0 0 1px accent is the selected card ring, and 0 ±2px 0 0 accent is the reorder drop line. Both draw a stroke outside the box without moving anything, because the border is already spoken for.

rules.name: The Load-Bearing Left Border Rule
rules.body: The 3px left border is the only place a card face changes shape, and it always encodes state — project, blocked, open reference, finished reference. It is not available for decoration or for a fifth meaning without retiring one of the four.

rules.name: The Dashed Means Absent Rule
rules.body: Dashed is reserved for a container whose value does not exist — the (none) column, a context-only canvas band. It never means draft, disabled or optional.

dos: Do claim a whole hue family when adding a facet axis, and take its text, -bg fill and 30–34% border together. A chip’s colour is its axis name.
Do put mono on anything the app says — labels, keys, counts, chips, column names, table headers — and sans on anything a human typed.
Do give every count font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums.
Do reach for the tonal stack before a shadow. ground → surface → surface-2 → surface-3 is four levels of depth and covers every case that is not literally floating.
Do reach for an existing --text-* step. Fourteen is already more than a scale needs; adding a fifteenth is a deliberate act that test/theme.test.ts will make you perform on purpose.
Do measure a glyph you place in a text run, and write the measurement down in a comment beside the constant.
Do clamp overlays with min(px, vw) when a window might be narrow.
Do let motion exist exactly where a mouse gesture would feel broken without it — dragging a card, panning or zooming the canvas, collapsing the rail. Regrouping, re-sorting and filtering are instant.
donts: Don’t animate a card, chip, column, panel or table. There are no keyframes in this system and no transition longer than 140ms, and both existing ones animate a width.

Don’t drift toward consumer SaaS polish: generous whitespace, 16px body type, large radii, gradients, illustrated empty states, spring easing. The working type size here is 12.5px and the largest radius is 10px, on purpose.
Don’t drift toward enterprise tracker chrome either: stacked toolbars, breadcrumbs, avatar rows, modal over modal, or status rendered as a filled pill competing for attention.
Don’t dress the terminal up. Xoria and the mono labels are a working grammar, not a costume — no ASCII borders, scanlines, CRT glow, blinking cursors or fixed 80-column measures.

Don’t use the accent for data structure. It marks live state and the app speaking, and nothing else. A record being a project is a property of the record, so .cardface.is-project draws its left border in hue-purple — the project axis’s own family — even though the two tokens hold the same value in both themes.

Don’t put --ink on a filled background. ink and the semantic hues follow the theme in the same direction, so the pair never has contrast: ink on bad measured 1.92:1 in light, and ink on warn 1.03:1 in dark — invisible. Every filled state takes ground, which is 7.58:1 at worst across the same four combinations, and is what .btn.primary and the two bucket chips do.
Don’t add a breakpoint. There are none, and the surface is a second monitor.

Don’t interpolate a colour. Every value comes from xoria256.yml; the two exceptions (rel-blocks at #b06060 in light, and the chip-tint mixes) are documented where they occur and each has a stated reason.
Don’t give a hint facet a diluted hue. It gets no hue, or it earns a family of its own.
Don’t nest a scroll inside a scroll. One region scrolls per axis.
Don’t use dashed borders for anything but a container whose value does not exist.
